project.name: eventsnare
project.description: Hosted webhook reliability service. Customers point third-party providers (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, Clerk, Resend) at an Eventsnare ingress URL; it verifies signatures, durably persists events, and reliably delivers them with retries, deduplication, and a one-click replay dashboard. Note: this project has over 100 source files; consider scoping analysis to a subdirectory for faster results.

tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Start with the README and the product spec to understand what Eventsnare is: a hosted webhook reliability service that verifies provider signatures, durably persists events, and delivers them to customer endpoints with retries, dedup, and replay. The README maps the Turborepo monorepo (landing, web, admin apps plus the Convex backend), while SPEC.md is the authoritative source for functional requirements, the data model, and the provider adapter contract referenced throughout the rest of this tour.

tour.title: Monorepo & Build Topology
tour.description: Before diving into code, see how the workspace fits together. The root package.json declares pnpm as the package manager and delegates dev/build/lint/typecheck to Turbo, and turbo.json defines the task graph and caching across all apps and packages. This explains why the backend, three frontends, and shared packages can be developed and built as one coordinated unit.
tour.languageLesson: Turborepo pipelines declare task dependencies (e.g. build dependsOn ^build) so upstream packages build before consumers, and content-hash caching skips unchanged work. pnpm workspaces link local packages by name without publishing.

tour.title: Ingress: The Trust Boundary
tour.description: This is where every webhook enters the system. http.ts is the Convex HTTP router registering all public routes (Clerk, Stripe, the per-source ingress endpoints, and waitlist). ingressHttp.ts implements the actual receiver: it reads the raw body, looks up the source, verifies the provider signature, and only then persists. This is the critical invariant in action: once a 2xx is returned to the provider, the event must already be durably stored.
tour.languageLesson: Convex HTTP Actions run in a single region and expose fetch-style handlers. The ingress action reads request.bytes() to preserve the body verbatim, since the forwarded request must be byte-for-byte identical to the original for downstream signature checks.

tour.title: The Provider Signature Library (The Moat)
tour.description: Signature verification is the highest-severity bug class in the codebase and the product's primary moat. types.ts defines the SPEC 7.3 ProviderAdapter contract (verifySignature, extractEventId, extractEventType), hmac.ts supplies the shared WebCrypto HMAC-SHA256 primitives and constant-time comparison, and index.ts is the registry that maps provider names to adapters. Building on the ingress flow from Step 3, this is the code that decides whether an incoming request is authentic.
tour.languageLesson: Signature comparison must be constant-time to avoid timing attacks: comparing byte-by-byte and returning early on the first mismatch leaks how much of the signature was correct. The hmac helper compares the full length regardless of where bytes differ.

tour.title: A Concrete Adapter: Stripe
tour.description: With the adapter contract understood, study a real implementation. The Stripe adapter parses the Stripe-Signature header (timestamp plus v1 schemes), reconstructs the signed payload, verifies the timestamped HMAC using the primitives from Step 4, and extracts the event id and type. Each launch provider (Stripe, GitHub, Shopify, Clerk, Resend) follows this same shape and is backed by a fixture test suite of captured real payloads.

tour.title: The Durable Data Model
tour.description: Once a signature is verified, the event must be persisted. schema.ts is the root Convex schema that composes per-domain table fragments into one defineSchema call, and ingress/schema.ts defines the core webhook tables: sources (provider + encrypted secret + forward URL), events (payload + signature status + lifecycle status), deliveryAttempts (per-retry records), and usageCounters. This is the durable backbone every other backend module reads and writes.
tour.languageLesson: The dedup invariant (source_id, provider_event_id) is enforced by a unique compound index where first write wins. Convex indexes are declared in the schema, and the ingress mutation relies on this index so duplicate provider retries collapse to a single event.

tour.title: Persisting Events with Dedup
tour.description: ingress.ts holds the mutations that the ingress HTTP action from Step 3 calls to durably write events: it enforces the (source_id, provider_event_id) dedup key, increments usage counters, and prepares the event for delivery. Because this mutation completes before the HTTP action returns 2xx, it is the linchpin of the 100%-durability-once-acknowledged guarantee.

tour.title: Reliable Delivery & Retries
tour.description: delivery.ts is the outbound worker that closes the loop: it resolves the delivery context for a queued event, performs a forwarding fetch with a 30s timeout, and records the attempt result, scheduling the next retry on the SPEC backoff schedule (10s, 30s, 2m, 10m, 1h, 6h, 24h) until dead-lettering after seven attempts. sources.ts manages the source records this depends on: CRUD, secret rotation, pause/resume, forward-URL validation, and test events.
tour.languageLesson: Convex schedules retries with ctx.scheduler.runAfter(delayMs, ...) rather than polling for due work. Each failed attempt self-schedules the next one with an increasing delay, making the backoff schedule fully event-driven.

tour.title: The Customer Dashboard
tour.description: Now switch to the customer-facing side. main.tsx mounts the web app, and App.tsx wires authentication, routing, and the feature route trees (events, sources, settings, billing, onboarding). The events.ts backend module exposes the queries and mutations these screens consume: listing and reading events, plus single and bulk replay into the delivery pipeline from Step 8. This is how customers observe and re-drive the reliability flow.

tour.title: Events, Sources & One-Click Replay
tour.description: These routes are the heart of the dashboard UX. EventsList provides status-filtered, paginated views of webhook events via a reactive Convex query; EventDetail shows the payload, the per-attempt delivery history from Step 8, and a replay control; ReplayButton triggers the replay mutation; and SourceDetail manages a source's lifecycle (pause, resume, delete, secret rotation, forward URL). Together they expose the durable pipeline as an operable product surface.
tour.languageLesson: Convex reactive queries replace SSE/WebSocket plumbing: a useQuery subscription re-renders automatically when the underlying tables change, so a delivery attempt recorded by the backend worker streams into the EventDetail view with no manual refresh.

tour.title: Auth, RBAC & Admin Console
tour.description: Finally, the access-control layer and internal tooling. ClerkProvider binds Clerk auth to the Convex client via ConvexProviderWithClerk; rbac.ts defines roles, permissions, and the requireRole/requirePermission guards enforced on the backend; and AdminGate guards the separate admin app, rendering an access-denied screen unless the user holds the admin role. This is how Eventsnare separates customer dashboards from the operator console while sharing one Convex backend.
